concepts.title: Linear probes
concepts.one_liner: Linear probes are lightweight linear modules added to a computation graph to repurpose a network for new tasks or to assess the knowledge represented in feature maps.
concepts.content: A model can be adapted by changing its parameters or by adding new modules to the computation graph. One important kind of new module is a read out module that takes features from the computation graph as input and produces a new prediction as output. When these modules are linear, they are called linear probes. These modules are relatively lightweight, having few parameters, and can be optimized with tools from linear optimization where closed form solutions are often available. Because of this, linear probes are very popular as a way of repurposing a neural net to perform a new task. These modules are also useful as a way of assessing what kind of knowledge each feature map in the original network represents; if a feature map can linearly classify some attribute of the data, then that feature map contains information about that attribute. In this usage, linear probes are probing the knowledge represented in some layer of a neural net.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear probes provide a computationally efficient way to adapt large pre-trained models to new tasks without retraining the entire network. They also serve as a diagnostic tool for researchers to interpret what specific layers of a neural network have learned about the data.
concepts.recap_md: - Linear probes are linear read-out modules added to a network to generate new predictions.

concepts.title: Learning from a teacher
concepts.one_liner: Learning from a teacher involves a student model observing a well-trained teacher model to imitate its outputs or match its intermediate processing.
concepts.content:
Supervised learning is often described as learning from examples, where a learner is given a dataset of input-output pairs to infer a relationship. This can be visualized as:

[FIGURE:bf8fbd1d5fd5a3e3]

This kind of learning is like having a teacher who provides an answer key but no explanations. Alternatively, we can consider a more instructive setting where the teacher is a well-trained model $t: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$ that maps input queries to output answers. The student (the learner) observes both data $\{x^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}$ and has access to the teacher model $t$. The student can learn to imitate the teacher's outputs or can learn to match how the teacher processes the queries by matching intermediate activations of the teacher model.

[FIGURE:872a10889f557ebb]

Learning from examples can be considered a special case of learning from a teacher where the teacher is the world and our only access is observing the outputs $y$ that match each input $x$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard supervised learning is limited to observing final labels. By treating a trained model as a teacher, a student model can leverage richer information, such as the teacher's internal logic or confidence levels, to learn more efficiently.
concepts.recap_md: - The student model learns by imitating the teacher model's outputs or intermediate activations.

key_passage.text: One way of formalizing this setting is to consider the teacher as a well-trained model $t: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$ that maps input queries to output answers. The student (the learner) observes both data $\{x^{(i)}\}^N_{i=1}$ and has access to the teacher model $t$. The student can learn to imitate the teacher's outputs or can learn to match *how the teacher processes the queries*, matching intermediate activations of the teacher model.

concepts.title: Knowledge distillation
concepts.one_liner: Knowledge distillation is an algorithm where a student model learns to imitate the probability mass function outputs of a well-trained teacher model.
concepts.content: Knowledge distillation is a simple and popular algorithm for learning a classifier from a teacher. We assume that the teacher is a well-trained classifier that outputs a $K-1$-dimensional probability mass function (pmf), $t: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \vartriangle^{K-1}$. The student, a model $f_{\theta}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \vartriangle^{K-1}$, simply tries to imitate the teacher's output pmf: for each input $x$ that the student sees, its goal is to output the same pmf vector as the teacher outputs for $x$.
concepts.motivation_md: Knowledge distillation allows a smaller, more efficient student model to capture the performance of a larger, complex teacher model by mimicking its soft probability distributions.
concepts.recap_md: - The student model $f_{\theta}$ aims to match the teacher's output probability mass function $t(x)$.

concepts.title: Knowledge distillation procedure
concepts.one_liner: Knowledge distillation involves training a student model to match the graded probability vectors of a teacher model rather than one-hot ground truth labels.
concepts.content:
Knowledge distillation is a simple and popular algorithm for learning a classifier from a teacher. We assume that the teacher is a well-trained classifier that outputs a $K-1$-dimensional probability mass function (pmf), $t: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \vartriangle^{K-1}$. The student, a model $f_{\theta}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \vartriangle^{K-1}$, simply tries to imitate the teacher's output pmf: for each input $x$ that the student sees, its goal is to output the same pmf vector as the teacher outputs for $x$. The full algorithm is given in the diagram below.

[FIGURE:d0121ab0dd8a499c]

This procedure was originally defined by Hinton et al. (2015), though the term now refers to a broader family of algorithms. This learning problem is similar to softmax regression on labeled data, but in knowledge distillation, the targets are not one-hot; they are more graded. The teacher outputs a probability vector reflecting its belief about the class of the input. These beliefs may assign partial credit to classes similar to the ground truth, which can make the teacher more informative than ground truth labels alone.

(see figure: Comparing knowledge distillation to supervised learning from labels.)
concepts.motivation_md: By using the teacher's soft probabilities (graded targets) instead of hard labels, the student learns about the relationships between classes, which provides a richer signal for training.
concepts.recap_md: - The student model imitates the teacher's full probability distribution rather than just the correct label.

concepts.title: Prompting
concepts.one_liner: Prompting edits the input data, such as by prepending text or visual information, to solve a new problem without changing the model's parameters.
concepts.content:
Prompting edits the input data to solve a new problem. In natural language processing (NLP), text-to-text systems can have natural language prompts prepended to the input string. For example, a general-purpose language model can be prompted with ["Make sure to answer in French", "X"], where the output will be a French translation of the response to "X".

The same can be done for vision systems. Prompting methods from NLP can be used for text inputs to vision-language models. Additionally, prompting can be applied to visual inputs, a method called visual prompting. This is done by concatenating pixels, tokens, or other visual formats to a vision model's inputs. This requires a model that takes variable-sized inputs, which includes most neural net architectures like CNNs, RNNs, and transformers. Alternatively, the visual prompt can be combined with the input query through addition.

Prompting is visualized in @fig-transfer_learning-prompting, where $\oplus$ represents concatenation, addition, or other ways of mixing prompts and input signals.

(see figure: Prompting: a prompt $\mathbf{p}$ is combined with the input $x$ to change the output $y$.)
concepts.motivation_md: Prompting allows a single fixed model to perform many different tasks simply by changing the input context, avoiding the need for expensive fine-tuning or task-specific architectures.
concepts.recap_md: - Prompting modifies the input signal (text or pixels) rather than the model parameters.

concepts.title: Visual prompting
concepts.one_liner: Visual prompting is a technique where visual data is added to a model's input to adapt its behavior.
concepts.content: Visual prompting is a method where a visual input is prepended or combined with visual data, such as by concatenating pixels or tokens, to adapt a vision model to a new task.
concepts.motivation_md: Visual prompting allows vision models to be repurposed for new tasks (like specific classification or segmentation) by only optimizing a small input signal rather than the entire model.
concepts.recap_md: - Visual prompting involves adding or concatenating visual information to the input of a vision model.

concepts.title: Visual prompting methods
concepts.one_liner: Visual prompting involves optimizing an input signal, such as pixels or tokens, to change a vision model's behavior for a specific task.
concepts.content:
There are several concrete ways to prompt a vision system. One way is to directly edit the input pixels, as shown in @fig-transfer_learning-pixel_prompt:

(see figure: A prompt can be made out of pixels: a prompt image (which looks like a border of noise here) is added to the input image in order to change the model's behavior. Three different prompts are shown...)

In this approach, a prompt image $\mathbf{p}$ is added to the input image $\mathbf{x}$. Although the prompt may look like noise, it is an optimized signal designed to change the model's behavior, such as making it predict a specific attribute. This is mathematically similar to adversarial noise, and was early on referred to as adversarial reprogramming. However, here the noise is intended to improve performance on a task of interest. Given $M$ training examples $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^M$, the prompt is learned via:
$$\begin{aligned} \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\mathbf{p}} \sum_{i=1}^M \mathcal{L}(f(\mathbf{x}^{(i)} + \mathbf{p}), \mathbf{y}^{(i)}) \end{aligned}$$

Alternatively, a prompt can be added to an intermediate feature space. For vision transformers, a learnable token can be used as a prompt. This token is concatenated to the input tokens representing image patches:

(see figure: Prompting a transformer with a learnable input token. The prompt token is mixed into the network via attention; therefore \textit{no} parameters of the original network have to be updated (see...)

The token is a $d$-dimensional code vector optimized to change the transformer's behavior. The attention mechanism allows all input tokens to attend to the prompt, which modulates the transformation applied in the first layer.
concepts.motivation_md: Visual prompting provides a way to adapt large pre-trained vision models to new datasets by optimizing only a small number of input parameters (pixels or tokens), which is much faster than fine-tuning.
concepts.recap_md: - Pixel-space prompting adds an optimized noise-like signal to the input image.

concepts.title: Promptable systems
concepts.one_liner: Promptable systems are models trained to adapt their behavior at test time based on human-interpretable prompts like text instructions or user-drawn strokes.
concepts.content: It is possible to train a model to be promptable, so that it adapts better to user prompts at test time. An advantage of this approach is the ability to train a model to understand human-interpretable prompts. For example, a model's behavior can be adapted based on text instructions or user-drawn strokes. Many systems that interactively adapt to user inputs are considered promptable systems. Many of these systems use the tools of conditional generative modeling to train models that are conditioned on user text instructions.
concepts.motivation_md: Training for promptability creates more flexible and user-friendly AI systems that can be controlled through natural interaction rather than technical parameter tuning.
concepts.recap_md: - Promptable systems are designed to adapt to human-interpretable inputs like text or drawings.

concepts.title: One-shot learning
concepts.one_liner: One-shot learning is the ability to learn to recognize a new concept after seeing it just once.
concepts.content: Deep learning systems are often criticized for being data hungry, requiring thousands of labeled examples to learn a concept like "dog." In contrast, humans possess the ability to learn to recognize a new kind of animal after seeing it just once. This ability is known as one-shot learning.
concepts.motivation_md: The goal of one-shot learning is to reduce the massive data requirements of neural networks, making AI more efficient and capable of learning from limited information, similar to human cognition.
concepts.recap_md: - The ability to learn a concept from a single labeled example.

concepts.title: Domain adaptation
concepts.one_liner: Domain adaptation refers to methods for adapting the training domain to be more like the test domain, or vice versa, to make their distributions identical.
concepts.content: Often, the data we train on comes from a different distribution, or domain, than the data we will encounter at test time. For example, a recognition system might be trained on internet photos but deployed on a self-driving car, where the imagery looks very different. Domain adaptation refers to methods for adapting the training domain to be more like the test domain, or vice versa. One option is to adapt the test data, ${\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{test}}^{(i)},\mathbf{y}_{\texttt{test}}^{(i)}}_{i=1}^N$, to look more like the training data so that the model $f$ works well on both. Alternatively, we can adapt the training data to look like the test data before training $f$. In either case, the goal is to make the distribution of test and train data identical, so that a method that works on one will work just as well on the other.
concepts.motivation_md: Machine learning models often fail when the 'domain' of the deployment data differs from the training data. Domain adaptation provides a framework to bridge this gap, ensuring that models remain effective even when the environment or data source changes.
concepts.recap_md: - Domain adaptation aligns the distributions of training and test data to improve model generalization.

concepts.title: Unsupervised domain adaptation
concepts.one_liner: Unsupervised domain adaptation aligns training and test distributions using unlabeled test inputs when labels are only available during training.
concepts.content:
Commonly, we only have access to labels at training time, but may have plentiful unlabeled inputs ${\mathbf{x}^{\prime}_i}_{i=1}^N$ at testing time. This setting is known as unsupervised domain adaptation. In this case, we cannot make use of test labels, but we can still align the test inputs to look like the training inputs (or vice versa). One way to do so is to use a generative adversarial network (GAN) that translates the data in one domain to look identically distributed as the data in the other domain.

(see figure: Unpaired domain adaptation via adversarial translation.)
concepts.motivation_md: In many real-world applications, it is easy to collect large amounts of data in a new environment but very expensive to label it. Unsupervised domain adaptation allows models to leverage this unlabeled data to adapt to new domains.
concepts.recap_md: - This method performs domain alignment using only unlabeled inputs from the target test domain.

Commonly, we only have access to labels at training time, but may have plentiful unlabeled inputs ${\mathbf{x}^{\prime}_i}_{i=1}^N$ at testing time. This setting is known as unsupervised domain adaptation. In this case, we cannot make use of test labels, but we can still align the test inputs to look like the training inputs (or vice versa). One way to do so is to use a generative adversarial network (GAN) that translates the data in one domain to look identically distributed as the data in the other domain.

concepts.title: Using generative models as data sources
concepts.one_liner: Generative models can serve as data sources for transfer learning by providing an unbounded supply of synthetic, manipulatable data.
concepts.content: Generative models produce synthetic data that looks like real data, an ability that is highly useful for transfer learning. Generative data is not just a cheap copy of real data; it can be "more" data and "better" data. It is "more" because we can draw an unbounded number of samples that interpolate and remix training data in novel ways. It is "better" because the data comes coupled with a generation procedure that has structure, such as latent variables, which can be exploited to manipulate the data distribution. For example, if a model is pretrained to produce images, one can edit its latent variables to generate specific scenarios—like cows on beaches—to adapt training data for new applications. In this usage, knowledge about data is transferred to accelerate learning for a new problem, leveraging the generative model's understanding of how the world looks.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard datasets are often limited or biased. Generative models allow us to synthesize an infinite variety of training examples, including rare edge cases, by manipulating the underlying variables of the data generation process.
concepts.recap_md: - Generative models provide an infinite source of synthetic data that goes beyond simple replication of training sets.

concepts.title: Learned loss

position.section_title: Other Kinds of Knowledge that Can Be Transferred

concepts.one_liner: A learned loss is a loss function that is itself pretrained to define the objective for a learning task.
concepts.content: A learned loss refers to the pretraining of the component that defines the loss function. Instead of using a standard, manually defined loss, this component is learned to optimize the training of a model.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard loss functions like MSE or Cross-Entropy may not be optimal for every task. Learning the loss function allows the system to discover a more effective objective for training.
concepts.recap_md: - A learned loss is a pretrained objective function used to guide the training of other models.

concepts.title: Learned optimizer

concepts.one_liner: A learned optimizer is an optimization algorithm that is pretrained to update model parameters more effectively than standard algorithms.
concepts.content: A learned optimizer is a component that defines the optimizer (such as SGD) and can be pretrained. While it is currently less common to adapt these modules—they are usually pretrained and then held fixed—there is no reason why they cannot be adapted in principle.

concepts.title: Transfer learning as empirical risk minimization

position.section_title: A Combinatorial Catalog of Transfer Learning Methods

concepts.one_liner: Many transfer learning methods can be framed as empirical risk minimization (ERM) where different components are optimized during pretraining or adaptation.
concepts.content:
Many transfer learning methods follow a similar format: pretrain one component of the system, then adapt that component and/or other components. These methods can be related by framing them as empirical risk minimization (ERM) with different components optimized during pretraining and/or during adaptation.

| Method | Learning | Inference |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Generative data | $\arg\min_{\textcolor{{rgb}{0.8, 0.0, 0.2}}{\theta}} \mathbb{E}_{\textcolor{pretrained_color}{x},\textcolor{pretrained_color}{y}}[\mathcal{L}(f_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}}(\textcolor{pretrained_color}{x}), \textcolor{pretrained_color}{y})]$ | $f_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}}(x)$ |
| Distillation | $\arg\min_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}} \mathbb{E}_{x}[\mathcal{L}(f_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}}(x), \textcolor{pretrained_color}{t}(x))]$ | $f_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}}(x)$ |
| Prompting | $\arg\min_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\epsilon}} \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\mathcal{L}(f_{\textcolor{pretrained_color}{\theta}}(x \oplus \textcolor{adapted_color}{\epsilon}), y)]$ | $f_{\textcolor{pretrained_color}{\theta}}(x \oplus \textcolor{adapted_color}{\epsilon})$ |
| Finetuning | $\arg\min_{\textcolor{both_color}{\theta}} \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\mathcal{L}(f_{\textcolor{both_color}{\theta}}(x), y)]$ | $f_{\textcolor{both_color}{\theta}}(x)$ |
| Probes / heads | $\arg\min_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\phi}} \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\mathcal{L}(h_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\phi}}(f_{\textcolor{pretrained_color}{\theta}}(x)), y)]$ | $h_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\phi}}(f_{\textcolor{pretrained_color}{\theta}}(x))$ |
| Learned loss | $\arg\min_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}} \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\textcolor{pretrained_color}{\mathcal{L}}(f_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}}(x), y)]$ | $f_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}}(x)$ |
| Learned optimizer | $\textcolor{pretrained_color}{\arg\min}_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}} \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\mathcal{L}(f_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}}(x), y)]$ | $f_{\textcolor{adapted_color}{\theta}}(x)$ |

Note: The $\oplus$ symbol indicates concatenation or addition. Domain adaptation does not map neatly to ERM and is omitted here.
concepts.motivation_md: Providing a unified mathematical framework for transfer learning allows researchers to categorize and compare diverse techniques like prompting and distillation using the common language of optimization.

concepts.title: Sequence Models from the Lens of Adaptation

position.section_title: Sequence Models from the Lens of Adaptation

concepts.one_liner: Sequence models like RNNs can be viewed as adaptation algorithms that update their behavior based on previously seen items in a sequence.
concepts.content: Sequence models, such as CNNs, transformers, and RNNs, can be considered adaptation algorithms because they update their behavior based on the items in the sequence they have already seen. This ability to handle adaptation is clearest with RNNs, which update their hidden states as they process data. These changes in hidden state modify the mapping from input to output, effectively allowing the model to adapt. Since learning is the problem of adapting future behavior as a function of past data, an RNN processing a sequence of training points can be viewed as performing learning.
concepts.motivation_md: Viewing sequence modeling as a form of adaptation helps explain how models like RNNs can 'learn' from context during inference, bridging the gap between static prediction and dynamic learning.
concepts.recap_md: - Sequence models adapt their behavior dynamically based on previously processed information in a sequence.

key_passage.text: RNNs update their hidden states as they process a sequence of data. These changes in hidden state change the behavior of the mapping from input to output. Therefore, RNNs adapt as they process data.

concepts.title: In-context learning

position.section_title: Sequence Models from the Lens of Adaptation

concepts.one_liner: In-context learning is a kind of learning, emergent in a sequence modeling problem, where a model performs supervised learning by processing a sequence of examples.
concepts.content: In-context learning is a phenomenon emergent in sequence modeling. In this framework, supervised learning is treated as the problem of taking a sequence of examples $\{\mathbf{x}^{(1)}, \mathbf{y}^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf{x}^{(n)}, \mathbf{y}^{(n)}\}$ as input to produce a function $f$ as output. For example, after an RNN processes this training sequence, it arrives at a specific hidden state. When the RNN is then fed a new query $\mathbf{x}^{(n+1)}$, the mapping it applies to produce an output $\mathbf{y}^{(n+1)}$ represents the learned function $f$. This function is defined by the parameters of the RNN along with the hidden state derived from the training sequence. Consequently, the RNN operates as a learning algorithm that can apply the inferred function to any arbitrary query.
concepts.motivation_md: In-context learning allows models to adapt to new tasks during inference without updating their internal weights, enabling flexible problem-solving based purely on the provided input sequence.
concepts.recap_md: - It treats a sequence of input-output pairs as training data to infer a specific function $f$.

key_passage.text: Another name for this kind of learning, which is emergent in a sequence modeling problem, is in-context learning.

motivation.text: The goal of supervised learning is that after training on the training data, we should do well on any random test query. After processing the training sequence, an RNN will have arrived at some setting of its hidden state. Now if we feed the RNN a new query, the mapping it applies, which produces an output, can be considered the learned function.

concepts.title: The problem setting for transfer learning
concepts.one_liner: Transfer learning is the study of how to use a previously trained classifier to accelerate the learning of a new classifier for a different task.
concepts.content: Suppose you are working at a farm and the drones that water the plants need to be able to recognize whether the crop is wheat or corn. Using the machinery we have learned so far, you know what to do: gather a big dataset of aerial photos of the crops and label each as either wheat or corn, then, train your favorite classifier to perform the mapping $f_{	heta}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \{\texttt{wheat}, \texttt{corn}\}$. It works! The crop yield is plentiful. Now a new season rolls around and it turns out the value of corn has plummeted. You decide to plant soybeans instead. So, you need a new classifier; what should you do? One option is to train a new classifier from scratch, this time on images of either wheat or soybeans. But you already know how to recognize wheat; you still have last year's classifier $f_{	heta}$. We would like to make use of $f_{	heta}$ to accelerate the learning of this year's new classifier. Transfer learning is the study of how to do this. Transfer learning algorithms involve two parts: 1. Pretraining: how to acquire prior knowledge in the first place. 2. Adaptation: how to use prior knowledge to solve a new task. In our example, the pretraining phase was training the wheat versus corn classifier, and the adaptation phase is updating that classifier to instead recognize wheat versus soybeans. This is visualized below in @fig-transfer_learning-finetuning_basic. (see figure: Transfer learning consists of two phases: first we pretrain a model on one task and then we adapt that model to perform a new task.)
concepts.motivation_md: Training models from scratch for every new task is computationally expensive and data-intensive; transfer learning leverages existing knowledge to solve new problems more efficiently.
concepts.recap_md: - Transfer learning leverages knowledge from a pretrained model to solve a new, related task. - The process is divided into two main phases: pretraining and adaptation.

concepts.title: Finetuning
concepts.one_liner: Finetuning consists of initializing a new classifier with the parameter vector from a pretrained model and then training it as usual.
concepts.content: Finetuning consists of initialializing a new classifier with the parameter vector from the pretrained model, and then training it as usual. In other words, finetuning is making small (fine) adjustments (tuning) to the parameters of your model to adapt it to do something slightly different than what it did before, or even something a lot different.
concepts.motivation_md: Finetuning provides a practical way to transfer knowledge by starting from a good set of weights rather than random initialization, leading to faster convergence and better performance.

concepts.title: Finetuning algorithm and layer replacement
concepts.one_liner: Finetuning involves initializing a model with pretrained parameters and replacing layers as needed to match the input or output dimensions of a new task.
concepts.content: Finetuning consists of initialializing a new classifier with the parameter vector from the pretrained model, and then training it as usual. There are three stages: (1) pretrain $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$, (2) initialize $f^{\prime} = f$, and (3) finetune $f^{\prime}: \mathcal{X}^{\prime} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}^{\prime}$. The full algorithm is written in @alg-transfer_learning-finetuning, with $f$ and $f^{\prime}$ indicated as just a continually learning $f_{\theta}$ with different iterates of $\theta$ as learning progresses. (see figure: Finetuning. Using gradient descent to train one model and then finetuning to produce a second model.) If the structure of $f_{\theta}$ is incompatible with the new problem, such as when the dimensionality of $\mathcal{X}$ or $\mathcal{Y}$ changes, it is common to cut off the last layer of the network and replace it with a new final layer that outputs the correct dimensionality. Both these changes are shown in @fig-transfer_learning-finetuning_stages.  To be precise, let $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$ decompose as $f= f_1 \circ f_2 \circ f_3$. To learn a function $f^{\prime}: \mathcal{X}^{\prime} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}^{\prime}$, we initialize $f^{\prime}_2$ with the parameters of $f_2$ and initialize $f^{\prime}_1$ and $f^{\prime}_3$ randomly.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard finetuning requires architectural consistency; layer replacement techniques allow transfer learning to be applied even when the number of classes or input formats change.
concepts.recap_md: - The finetuning algorithm involves pretraining, initializing with those weights, and then training on the new task. - Incompatible layers, such as the input or output layers, are replaced and trained from scratch.

key_passage.text: Finetuning consists of initialializing a new classifier with the parameter vector from the pretrained model, and then training it as usual. In other words, finetuning is making small (fine) adjustments (tuning) to the parameters of your model to adapt it to do something slightly different than what it did before, or even something a lot different.

concepts.title: Finetuning subparts of a network
concepts.one_liner: Selectively finetuning some layers while freezing others allows for composing pretrained modules and preventing the loss of prior knowledge.
concepts.content: You don't have to finetune all layers in your network but can selectively finetune some and initialize others from scratch. This strategy allows initializing some parts of a computation graph from pretrained models while others are trained from scratch. Sometimes you may want to *freeze* certain layers to prevent them from forgetting their prior knowledge. An example is given in @fig-transfer_learning-finetuning_certain_modules_example for a car detection system. The `featurize` module converts the input image $\mathbf{x}$ into a feature map and is pretrained and frozen. Next, the `depth estimator` and `dense classifier` modules are finetuned to work on specific street images. Finally, the `detector` module outputs a bounding box $\mathbf{y}$. We use the symbol [FIGURE:29db42ece472b20d] to indicate a frozen module and the symbol [FIGURE:9ec05bcb43ceee69] to indicate a module that is updated during adaptation. (see figure: Finetuning certain subsets of a computation graph. Here we show some modules that have been pretrained (those with a shaded background) and one that is trained from scratch at finetuning time.) Within a single layer, it is also possible to update just a subspace of the full weight matrix, such as by applying a low-rank update.
concepts.motivation_md: Selective finetuning and freezing prevent catastrophic forgetting and reduce the computational cost of training large models on specific tasks.
concepts.recap_md: - Specific modules in a computation graph can be frozen to retain their pretrained knowledge during adaptation. - Selective finetuning allows for combining pretrained components with new, task-specific layers. - Low-rank updates can be used to adapt weight matrices efficiently.

key_passage.text: you don't have to finetune all layers in your network but can selectively finetune some and initialize others from scratch. In fact this strategy can be applied quite generally, where we initialize some parts of a computation graph from pretrained models and initialize others from scratch.

motivation.text: Sometimes you might have pretrained models that can perform just certain parts of what your full system needs to do. You can use these pretrained models and compose them together with layers initialized from scratch. Other times you may want to freeze certain layers to prevent them from forgetting their prior knowledge.

prereq.rationale: Pretraining is defined as the initial stage of the transfer learning workflow described in the problem setting.
Adaptation is the application of knowledge, which logically necessitates that the knowledge was first acquired through pretraining.
Adaptation is the specific step in the transfer learning problem where the agent applies old knowledge to a new task.
Finetuning is defined by the process of starting from a model that has already undergone pretraining.
The finetuning technique provides the algorithmic implementation of the finetuning concept.
Selective finetuning is a more granular application of the general finetuning algorithm.
The procedure is the algorithmic implementation of the knowledge distillation definition.
The definition of a learned loss explicitly involves the pretraining of the component that defines the loss.
The concept defines sequence models specifically through the lens of adaptation, viewing their state updates as a form of behavioral change.
In-context learning is presented as a specific phenomenon emergent from the adaptation capabilities of sequence models.
Prompting is a method of adapting a model to a new task by editing input data rather than parameters.
The technique of visual prompting implements the definition by optimizing input signals like pixels.
Promptable systems are specifically trained to be used with prompting techniques at test time.

overlay.rationale: Unsupervised domain adaptation is the specific setting of domain adaptation where labels are unavailable for the test domain.
Finetuning is a specific method used to adapt a model to a new task or domain.
Linear probes provide a lightweight mechanism for adapting a pretrained network to a new task.
Knowledge distillation is a specific algorithm that implements the broader concept of learning from a teacher model.
Few-shot learning is the broader category of learning from a small number of examples, of which one-shot is the N=1 case.
Zero-shot learning is the extreme case where no examples are provided, contrasting with the few examples required in few-shot learning.
Generative data methods are explicitly mapped to the ERM framework in the provided table.
Knowledge distillation is used as a concrete example of a transfer learning method that can be framed as ERM.
Prompting is contrasted with finetuning because it does not involve updating the model's weights.
Visual prompting is a specific application of the general prompting technique to visual data.
Generating specific scenarios to adapt training data for new applications is a practical application of domain adaptation.
